title: Project Overview
description: Start with the README to see GroundMark’s purpose: turning scanned PDFs and images into layout-aware Markdown while keeping page, block, and bounding-box structure. It also introduces the UI and CLI workflows, configuration, exports, and document chat, giving context for the components that follow.

title: User Entry Points
description: Building on the workflows introduced in Step 1, the Streamlit app and CLI expose document parsing and pipeline runs to users. The app delegates parsing and rendering to application modules, while the CLI provides terminal-oriented commands into the same project capabilities.

title: Document Inputs and Types
description: Before layout analysis, preprocessing normalizes PDFs and images by rasterizing pages, resizing images, and preparing model-ready data. Pydantic models define the shared shapes for bounding boxes, layout blocks, parsed pages, and chat messages, so downstream parsing and presentation work against explicit contracts.

title: Layout and Reading Order
description: With normalized pages and typed structures in place, the layout engine identifies blocks, columns, headers, tables, bounding boxes, and reading order. This is a central part of GroundMark’s output: it preserves document structure instead of reducing a page to an undifferentiated text string.

title: Vision Prompt and Client
description: The layout workflow pairs runtime instructions for page analysis with a client wrapper that handles model access, structured outputs, and retries. The prompt defines the requested structure, while the client provides the boundary for sending inference requests and receiving responses for the parsing pipeline.

title: Parsing Pipeline
description: The parsing facade coordinates document preparation, model inference, and output formatting, bringing together the earlier input and layout stages. The LangGraph runner organizes execution as a preprocess-to-parse flow with isolated run state, option validation, progress updates, and returned status and artifacts.

title: Rendered Exports
description: Once parsing produces a result, the Markdown renderer converts structured blocks into escaped Markdown and HTML, including tables, lists, headings, and figure links. Export coordination can write multiple artifact formats from that result, while figure handling verifies source-matched crops and treats unavailable images as warnings rather than discarding the extraction.

title: Grounded Document Chat
description: Alongside extraction, the chat module supports multi-turn questions over parsed documents with citation verification and structured reasoning. The feature guide explains the evidence boundary: chat uses successfully parsed pages, checks quoted support and citations, and fails closed when an answer cannot be grounded.

title: Diagnostics and Usage
description: Parsing and chat depend on remote model calls, so diagnostics classify API health and errors, record token usage, and identify content-filter outcomes. The usage ledger tracks prompt and completion tokens and estimates cost, making operational information available without changing the document structure contract.

title: Architecture Map
description: After following the implementation from entry points through parsing, exports, and chat, use the architecture guide to connect those parts into one system view. It summarizes the UI and CLI paths, document structures, rendering and export behavior, and the boundary between extraction and chat.

title: Regression Test Contracts
description: The tests turn key pipeline expectations into repeatable checks: layout tests cover hierarchy and reading order, graph tests cover run lifecycle and artifact behavior, and CLI tests cover extraction and export options. A deterministic fake LLM keeps these paths testable without relying on live model responses, complementing the contracts introduced in Steps 3–9.

title: Wiki Refresh Workflow
description: The repository’s documentation workflow is a maintenance capstone rather than part of document processing: it refreshes OpenWiki on a schedule or manual dispatch and proposes generated changes through a pull request. Its run-state cleanup and failure reporting show how the project keeps generated documentation updates separate from the runtime pipeline.
